newsitem.title: USA: Summit Technology dismisses founder chairman.
newsitem.headline: Summit Technology dismisses founder chairman.

text.p: Summit Technology Inc., a money-losing maker of devices to treat common vision problems, said Friday that its board dismissed company founder David Muller as chairman and chief executive.

Summit, which makes a pioneering laser device for eye surgery that was developed by Muller, said the board established a new executive committee chaired by President Verne Sharma, who will also serve as interim CEO.
The executive committee was formed to "identify and evaluate strategic options designed to achieve profitability," the company said in a statement.
The 47-year-old Muller's departure follows big financial losses at Summit, a sharp decline in its stock, shareholder lawsuits and a dispute with rival VISX Inc.
The company's stock, which traded at $34 at the start of the year, traded Friday morning at $6.3125, up 50 cents, on the Nasdaq market.
Muller developed a laser that treats nearsightedness by slicing off a thin layer of the eye's cornea, which can eliminate the need for eyeglasses.
However, the surgical procedure, which costs about $4,000, has not been well received by potential patients and the company sold few of the machines to doctors.
Muller could not be reached for comment.

Richard Miller, a board member speaking on behalf of the directors, said in a statement: "It is now time for the company to focus on the bottom line. We believe that Mr. Sharma and his team have the ability to accomplish our goals.
"I am confident that we can create a successful company and realise our goal of commercializing laser vision correction technology and bringing its benefits to millions of people worldwide."
The company, which also sells contact lenses and related products through a subsidiary, posted a net loss of $15.5 million in the first half of this year after losing $3.5 million last year.
Last month, a class action lawsuit was filed against Summit on behalf of shareholders alleging illegal sales of the laser that treats nearsightedness.

The suit also charged that Muller had received confidential and proprietary information about a similar laser made by VISX and, based on that non-public information, Muller and other top officers unloaded millions of dollars worth of Summit stock.
